kangaroo-at-2013-kadett-01.title: Count small triangles
kangaroo-at-2013-kadett-01.body:
The lines cut the big triangle into $3^2 = 9$ small equilateral triangles, all congruent, so each has area $9 \div 9 = 1$.

The grey part consists of three rhombi (top, bottom-left, bottom-right), each made of 2 small triangles: $3 \times 2 = 6$ small triangles.

Grey area $= 6$.

**Answer: (D) 6**

kangaroo-at-2013-kadett-01.title: Count the white part
kangaroo-at-2013-kadett-01.body:
Only 3 of the 9 small triangles are white (the two in the middle row beside the top rhombus and the one in the bottom middle). Grey $= 9 - 3 = 6$.

**Answer: (D) 6**

kangaroo-at-2013-kadett-03.title: Parts of the whole
kangaroo-at-2013-kadett-03.body:
Sea water has $7 + 193 = 200$ parts, of which 7 are salt. In 1000 kg each part is $1000 \div 200 = 5$ kg, so salt is $7 \times 5 = 35$ kg.

**Answer: (A) 35**

kangaroo-at-2013-kadett-03.title: Percent
kangaroo-at-2013-kadett-03.body:
Salt is $\frac{7}{200} = 3.5\%$ of the sea water, and $3.5\%$ of 1000 kg is 35 kg.

**Answer: (A) 35**

kangaroo-at-2013-kadett-04.title: Four pieces don't fit, three do
kangaroo-at-2013-kadett-04.body:
Each shape uses 4 squares. Four shapes would cover all 16 squares – let's see that this is impossible.

Look at the top-left corner square. Say a shape covers it lying horizontally: it covers the two left squares of the top row and the 2nd and 3rd squares of the second row. Now the square below the corner (row 2, column 1) can only be covered together with the square below it, by an upright shape going down to rows 3 and 4 – and that leaves the bottom-left corner square cut off with no free neighbour. If the corner shape stands upright, the same happens by symmetry. So the corner can never be covered in a complete tiling, and at most 3 shapes fit.

Three shapes do fit, e.g. (rows from top, columns from left): {r1c1, r1c2, r2c2, r2c3}, {r2c1, r3c1, r3c2, r4c2}, {r2c4, r3c3, r3c4, r4c3}.

Left over: $16 - 3 \cdot 4 = 4$ squares.

**Answer: (C) 4**

kangaroo-at-2013-kadett-06.title: Worst case
kangaroo-at-2013-kadett-06.body:
With bad luck, the first 5 marbles could all have different colours (one of each colour). The 6th marble must then repeat a colour, since there are only 5 colours.

So 6 marbles are needed, and 5 are not enough.

**Answer: (E) 6**

kangaroo-at-2013-kadett-07.title: List the candles
kangaroo-at-2013-kadett-07.body:
Candles are lit at minutes 0, 10, 20, 30, 40, 50 (by minute 55). A candle lit at minute $t$ burns until minute $t + 40$.

- lit at 0 → out at 40; lit at 10 → out at 50: both are out at minute 55.
- lit at 20, 30, 40, 50 → out at 60, 70, 80, 90: still burning.

4 candles are burning.

**Answer: (C) 4**

kangaroo-at-2013-kadett-07.title: Look back 40 minutes
kangaroo-at-2013-kadett-07.body:
At minute 55, the burning candles are exactly those lit in the last 40 minutes, i.e. after minute 15: at 20, 30, 40, 50 – four candles.

**Answer: (C) 4**

kangaroo-at-2013-kadett-08.title: The total must be a whole number
kangaroo-at-2013-kadett-08.body:
Average $=$ (total number of children) $\div 5$, so total $= 5 \times$ average must be a whole number.

- $5 \times 1.0 = 5$, $5 \times 1.2 = 6$, $5 \times 1.4 = 7$, $5 \times 2.0 = 10$ – fine.
- $5 \times 1.3 = 6.5$ – impossible.

**Answer: (C) 1.3**

kangaroo-at-2013-kadett-09.title: Gaining half a lap
kangaroo-at-2013-kadett-09.body:
Tom starts half a lap behind Laura. While Laura runs 8 parts of distance, Tom runs 9 parts, so he gains $\frac18$ of whatever Laura runs.

He needs to gain $\frac12$ lap: $\frac18 \cdot L = \frac12$ gives $L = 4$ laps for Laura.

**Answer: (A) 4**

kangaroo-at-2013-kadett-09.title: Count laps
kangaroo-at-2013-kadett-09.body:
When Laura has run 4 laps, Tom has run $\frac98 \cdot 4 = 4.5$ laps – exactly the half lap he was behind. Earlier he cannot catch her, since he gains only gradually.

**Answer: (A) 4**

kangaroo-at-2013-kadett-10.title: Use prime factors
kangaroo-at-2013-kadett-10.body:
$y$ divides both 14 and 10, so $y = 1$ or $2$; with $y = 1$ we would need $x = 14$, $z = 10$, but then $zx = 140 \ne 35$. So $y = 2$, $x = 7$, $z = 5$, and $zx = 35$ ✓. Sum $= 14$.

**Answer: (C) 14**

kangaroo-at-2013-kadett-11.title: Cross out forbidden squares
kangaroo-at-2013-kadett-11.body:
Number rows 1–5 from the top and columns 1–5 from the left. The ships occupy r2c1 and r4c2, r5c2.

Forbidden are the ship squares and all squares touching them (also diagonally): rows 1–3 in columns 1–2 (around the small ship) and rows 3–5 in columns 1–3 (around the long ship).

Free squares:
- rows 1 and 2: columns 3, 4, 5
- rows 3, 4, 5: columns 4, 5

Positions for a 3×1 ship:
- horizontal: row 1 (c3–c5) and row 2 (c3–c5): 2 positions;
- vertical in column 4: rows 1–3, 2–4, 3–5: 3 positions;
- vertical in column 5: 3 positions;
- column 3 has only 2 free squares.

Total $2 + 3 + 3 = 8$.

**Answer: (E) 8**

kangaroo-at-2013-kadett-12.title: Two triangles
kangaroo-at-2013-kadett-12.body:
The lines with angles $\alpha$ and $\beta$ form a triangle with the horizontal line. Its third angle (where the rising line meets the falling line) is $180^\circ - 55^\circ - 40^\circ = 85^\circ$.

Now look at the upper small triangle formed by the steep line, the falling line and the rising line. Its angle at the meeting point of the rising and falling line is the supplement $180^\circ - 85^\circ = 95^\circ$, and its angle at the top is $\gamma = 35^\circ$.

$\delta$ is the exterior angle of this small triangle at its third vertex, so it equals the sum of the two opposite interior angles:

$$\delta = 95^\circ + 35^\circ = 130^\circ.$$

**Answer: (E) 130°**

kangaroo-at-2013-kadett-12.title: Angle sum in the small triangle
kangaroo-at-2013-kadett-12.body:
The small upper triangle has angles $\gamma = 35^\circ$ at the top and $95^\circ$ (found as above) where the rising and falling lines meet. Its third angle, at the crossing of the steep line and the rising line, is $180^\circ - 35^\circ - 95^\circ = 50^\circ$. The angle $\delta$ lies next to it on a straight line, so $\delta = 180^\circ - 50^\circ = 130^\circ$.

**Answer: (E) 130°**

kangaroo-at-2013-kadett-13.title: Find the side lengths
kangaroo-at-2013-kadett-13.body:
Four whole-number sides adding to 5 must be $1, 1, 1, 2$.

The two parallel sides can't both be 1 (then the shape would be a parallelogram, whose opposite sides 1 and 2 would have to be equal). So the parallel sides are 2 and 1 and the legs are 1 and 1.

Put the short side 1 centred above the long side 2: each leg sticks out $\frac12$ horizontally and has length 1. A right triangle with hypotenuse 1 and adjacent side $\frac12$ has angle $60^\circ$ (it is half of an equilateral triangle).

So the angles are $60^\circ, 60^\circ, 120^\circ, 120^\circ$ – the trapezium is half of a regular hexagon.

**Answer: (B) 60° and 60°**

kangaroo-at-2013-kadett-13.title: Three equilateral triangles
kangaroo-at-2013-kadett-13.body:
With sides $2, 1, 1, 1$: cut the trapezium from the ends of the top side to the midpoint of the bottom side. You get three triangles with all sides 1 – equilateral. So the angles at the long base are $60^\circ$.

**Answer: (B) 60° and 60°**

kangaroo-at-2013-kadett-14.title: How the triangles must fit
kangaroo-at-2013-kadett-14.body:
Each shape is a row of 4 squares (which fold into the 4 side faces of a cube) plus four half-square triangles, two above and two below the row. The two triangles above must fold onto the top face and together cover it, so they must be the two halves of the top face cut along **one** diagonal.

When the row is folded into a ring, square 1 and square 4 become neighbours: the left edge of square 1 meets the right edge of square 4.

In Shape 3 the top triangles sit on squares 1 and 4, and both have their right angle at the outer ends of the row – which is the same corner of the top face after folding. Two right triangles with the right angle at the same corner are the same half of the face: they overlap and leave the other half uncovered. The same happens at the bottom.

Checking the other four shapes in the same way, their two triangles on each side are the two different halves of the face, so they fold into a cube.

**Answer: (C) Shape 3**

kangaroo-at-2013-kadett-15.title: Odd and even almost balance
kangaroo-at-2013-kadett-15.body:
In a run of consecutive whole numbers, odd and even numbers alternate, so the number of odd ones differs from the number of even ones by at most 1.

- 40%: 2 odd of 5 numbers (e.g. 2, 3, 4, 5, 6). ✓
- 48%: 12 odd of 25 numbers. ✓
- 50%: e.g. 1, 2. ✓
- 60%: 3 of 5 (e.g. 1, 2, 3, 4, 5). ✓
- 45% $= \frac{9}{20}$: with $n$ numbers, $0.45n$ must be a whole number, so $n$ is a multiple of 20. Then there would be $0.45n$ odd and $0.55n$ even numbers, a difference of $0.1n \ge 2$. Impossible.

**Answer: (B) 45%**

kangaroo-at-2013-kadett-17.title: Look where the first digit changes
kangaroo-at-2013-kadett-17.body:
The numbers start with 1, 2 or 3 (not 0). Inside a group with the same first digit, the numbers are close together; the big jumps are between groups:

- largest starting with 1: 1320; smallest starting with 2: 2013. Difference 693.
- largest starting with 2: 2310; smallest starting with 3: 3012. Difference **702**.

Inside a group, the largest jump comes when the second digit changes, e.g. $1032 \to 1203$ (171), $2031 \to 2103$ (72), $3021 \to 3102$ (81) – all smaller.

**Answer: (A) 702**

kangaroo-at-2013-kadett-18.title: Count the cut squares
kangaroo-at-2013-kadett-18.body:
A diagonal of a $10 \times 6$ grid goes from $(0,0)$ to $(10,6)$. It passes through the lattice point $(5,3)$ and nowhere else in between (since $\gcd(10,6) = 2$). So it consists of two copies of the diagonal of a $5\times3$ grid, each cutting $5 + 3 - 1 = 7$ squares: 14 squares per diagonal.

The two diagonals cross exactly at the grid point $(5,3)$, and near it they run through different squares (one through the lower-left and upper-right squares at that point, the other through the other two). They never share a square, so $2 \times 14 = 28$ squares are cut.

Uncut: $60 - 28 = 32$.

(Check with the $8\times6$ grid: each diagonal cuts $2\cdot(4+3-1) = 12$ squares, $48 - 24 = 24$ ✓.)

**Answer: (E) 32**

kangaroo-at-2013-kadett-19.title: Use the months first
kangaroo-at-2013-kadett-19.body:
The dates are: 20 Feb, 12 Mar, 20 Mar, 12 Apr, 23 Apr.

Two pairs share a month, so the two March dates and the two April dates are taken by the pairs (Andi, Edi) and (Berti, Christa). The lonely February date belongs to Doris: **Doris – 20 Feb**.

Edi has the same day as Doris, so **Edi – 20 Mar**, and Andi (same month as Edi) – **12 Mar**.

Christa has the same day as Andi in another month: **Christa – 12 Apr**, so **Berti – 23 Apr**.

The youngest child is the one born last: Berti.

**Answer: (B) Berti**

kangaroo-at-2013-kadett-21.title: As few digits as possible
kangaroo-at-2013-kadett-21.body:
No one-digit number has digit product 24. Two-digit numbers with digit product 24: $24 = 3\cdot8 = 4\cdot6$, giving 38, 83, 46, 64. The smallest is 38 (any number with more digits is bigger).

Digit sum: $3 + 8 = 11$.

**Answer: (E) 11**

kangaroo-at-2013-kadett-22.title: Signs and sizes
Slopes
kangaroo-at-2013-kadett-22.body:
$\frac{y}{x}$ is the slope of the line from the origin to the point. The steepest downward line from the origin to the rectangle goes to its lowest-left corner, $A$.

**Answer: (A) A**

kangaroo-at-2013-kadett-23.title: Rectangle minus corners
kangaroo-at-2013-kadett-23.body:
Use grid units (1 unit = 2 cm, 1 square unit = 4 cm²) with the bottom-left grid corner as origin. Reading the picture: $A = (2, 2)$, $B = (5, 1)$, $C = (8, 5)$, $D = (1, 6)$.

The surrounding rectangle from $x = 1$ to 8 and $y = 1$ to 6 has area $7 \times 5 = 35$. Cut away:
- top: triangle $D, C, (8,6)$: $\frac12 \cdot 7 \cdot 1 = 3.5$
- right: triangle $C, B, (8,1)$: $\frac12 \cdot 3 \cdot 4 = 6$
- left: triangle $D, A, (1,2)$: $\frac12 \cdot 1 \cdot 4 = 2$
- bottom left: the unit square from $(1,1)$ to $(2,2)$: 1, and triangle $A, B, (2,1)$: $\frac12\cdot3\cdot1 = 1.5$

Area $= 35 - 14 = 21$ square units $= 21 \times 4 = 84$ cm².

**Answer: (B) 84 cm²**

kangaroo-at-2013-kadett-24.title: Look at the units digit
kangaroo-at-2013-kadett-24.body:
If Robert removed any digit except the last one, both numbers would end in the same digit $u$, and the sum would end in the last digit of $2u$ – an even digit. But 52713 ends in 3. So he removed the **last** digit $d$.

Then the five-digit number is $10M + d$, where $M$ is the four-digit number, and

$$10M + d + M = 11M + d = 52713.$$

$52713 = 11 \cdot 4792 + 1$, so $M = 4792$, $d = 1$, and the original number is $47921$.

Digit sum: $4 + 7 + 9 + 2 + 1 = 23$.

**Answer: (C) 23**

kangaroo-at-2013-kadett-25.title: Split into four chains
kangaroo-at-2013-kadett-25.body:
"Three trees between them" means the positions differ by 4. Split the positions 1–20 into four chains:

$$1, 5, 9, 13, 17 \quad 2, 6, 10, 14, 18 \quad 3, 7, 11, 15, 19 \quad 4, 8, 12, 16, 20.$$

In each chain, neighbours differ by 4, so no two neighbours in a chain can both be oaks. In a chain of 5, that allows at most 3 oaks (positions 1st, 3rd, 5th). So at most $4 \times 3 = 12$ oaks.

12 is possible: oaks at 1–4, 9–12, 17–20, lindens at 5–8 and 13–16.

**Answer: (C) 12**

kangaroo-at-2013-kadett-26.title: Set up the equations
kangaroo-at-2013-kadett-26.body:
Alex is 21st, so 20 runners are before Alex. Then $1.5 \times 20 = 30$ runners are behind Daniel.

Let $N$ be the number of runners. Daniel's place is $N - 30$, so $N - 31$ runners are before Daniel. Behind Alex are $N - 21$ runners. The condition says

$$N - 21 = 2(N - 31) \Rightarrow N = 41.$$

Check: Daniel is 11th, 10 before him; 20 behind Alex $= 2 \cdot 10$ ✓; 30 behind Daniel $= 1.5 \cdot 20$ ✓.

**Answer: (B) 41**

kangaroo-at-2013-kadett-26.title: Test the options
kangaroo-at-2013-kadett-26.body:
Behind Daniel are always 30, so Daniel is at place $N - 30$.
- $N = 31$: Daniel 1st, 0 before him, behind Alex 10 ≠ 0. ✗
- $N = 41$: Daniel 11th, 10 before him, behind Alex 20 $= 2\cdot10$ ✓.

**Answer: (B) 41**

kangaroo-at-2013-kadett-27.title: Find the period
kangaroo-at-2013-kadett-27.body:
Continue: 6th $= 1 \cdot (-1) = -1$, 7th $= (-1)(-1) = 1$, 8th $= -1$, …

The sequence is $1, -1, -1,\ 1, -1, -1,\ \dots$ – it repeats in blocks of three with block sum $-1$.

$2013 = 3 \times 671$, so the sum is $671 \times (-1) = -671$.

**Answer: (B) −671**

kangaroo-at-2013-kadett-28.title: The pancakes form a pile
kangaroo-at-2013-kadett-28.body:
The hottest pancake is the most recently made one that is still there – the pancakes behave like a pile where you always take from the top.

Check (D) 456231: pancakes 1–4 are made and 4 is eaten; then 5 is made and eaten, then 6. Now 1, 2, 3 are left, and the hottest is 3. But the next one eaten is 2 – impossible.

The others work, e.g. (C) 325461: make 1, 2, 3; eat 3, eat 2; make 4, 5; eat 5, eat 4; make 6; eat 6; eat 1.

**Answer: (D) 456231**

kangaroo-at-2013-kadett-29.title: Add all labels
kangaroo-at-2013-kadett-29.body:
Let the vertex numbers sum to $S$. Each vertex lies on 3 edges, so the edge numbers sum to $3S$. All ten labels together:

$$S + 3S = 4S = 1 + 2 + \dots + 9 + 11 = 56 \Rightarrow S = 14.$$

$AB = a + b = 9$, so $CD = c + d = 14 - 9 = 5$.

(It really works: vertices $A = 2$, $B = 7$, $C = 1$, $D = 4$ give edges 9, 3, 6, 8, 11, 5.)

**Answer: (B) 5**

kangaroo-at-2013-kadett-30.title: No car leaves where it came in
kangaroo-at-2013-kadett-30.body:
Since no car drives all the way round, no car leaves at its own entrance. Each exit is used by exactly one car. So we need the arrangements of 4 cars to 4 exits where no car gets its own – the derangements of 4.

Count: total $4! = 24$ arrangements. Use inclusion–exclusion on cars that get their own exit:

$$24 - \binom41 3! + \binom42 2! - \binom43 1! + \binom44 0! = 24 - 24 + 12 - 4 + 1 = 9.$$

**Answer: (A) 9**

kangaroo-at-2013-kadett-30.title: List them
kangaroo-at-2013-kadett-30.body:
Call the cars 1, 2, 3, 4 with entrances 1, 2, 3, 4. Car 1 can take exit 2, 3 or 4 – three choices, and by symmetry each gives the same number of ways. If car 1 takes exit 2: either car 2 takes exit 1 (then cars 3, 4 must swap: 1 way) or car 2 takes exit 3 or 4 (then the rest is forced: 2 ways). So 3 ways per choice, $3 \times 3 = 9$ in total.

**Answer: (A) 9**
